content: Venous ulcers, also known as chronic venous ulcers, develop as a result of malfunctioning venous valves. These defective valves lead to blood backflow and pooling, or stasis, within the veins. This condition is most commonly observed in the legs. The management of venous ulcers involves a multifaceted approach, including patient education, leg elevation, elastic compression therapy, and regular evaluation. Antibiotic therapy is reserved for ulcers that have become secondarily infected. Venous ulcers are chronic wounds that arise due to improper functioning of the venous valves, which are responsible for preventing blood from flowing backward. These ulcers account for 70% to 90% of all chronic wound cases, making them a significant cause of chronic wounds. The pathophysiology of venous ulcers is complex and not fully understood. However, it is believed that these ulcers occur when venous valves fail to function properly, leading to increased venous pressure, or venous hypertension. Normally, the heart relies on a pressure gradient between arteries and veins to pump blood effectively. When venous hypertension occurs, this gradient diminishes, impairing blood flow into and out of the affected area and causing blood to pool. Venous hypertension can also stretch the veins, allowing blood proteins to leak into the surrounding tissue (extravascular space). This leakage isolates extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules and growth factors, preventing them from contributing to wound healing. Additionally, fibrinogen leakage and impaired fibrinolysis can lead to fibrin accumulation around blood vessels, which blocks oxygen and nutrients from reaching cells. Venous insufficiency may also cause white blood cells (leukocytes) to accumulate in small blood vessels. These leukocytes release inflammatory factors and reactive oxygen species (ROS), exacerbating chronic wound formation. The buildup of leukocytes can also obstruct small blood vessels, contributing to ischemia. This blockage may explain the no-reflow phenomenon, where ischemic tissue fails to regain adequate blood flow even after the obstruction is removed. Elevating the affected limb can help blood flow back into the area, but this may also contribute to reperfusion injury. Other comorbidities may also play a role in the development of venous ulcers. Treatment of venous ulcers is challenging and costly, with a high recurrence rate. Studies have shown that up to 48% of venous ulcers recur within five years of healing. For infected ulcers, preferred antibiotic regimens include Ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours. Alternative regimens include Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily or Levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily, combined with Metronidazole 500 mg orally four times daily. Another alternative involves Cefepime 2 g IV every 12 hours or Ceftazidime 2 g IV every 8 hours, combined with Metronidazole 500 mg orally four times daily. If gram-positive cocci are identified on gram stain, Vancomycin should be added. For inflamed ulcers, parenteral antibiotics are recommended, with no topical treatment. For non-inflamed ulcers, debridement, removal of foreign bodies, pressure reduction for weight-bearing limbs, and leg elevation are advised. Healing may be improved with the use of air beds, protein supplementation, radiant heat, and electrical stimulation. Chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine should be avoided as they may damage granulation tissue. The Bisgaard regimen is a widely used approach for treating venous ulcers. It is summarized by the mnemonic 4 E's: education, elevation, elastic compression, and evaluation. Compression therapy is a cornerstone of venous ulcer management. Non-elastic, below-knee compression systems are particularly effective in countering venous reflux and pump failure. Compression therapy reduces venous diameter and pressure, improving blood flow and preventing backflow. It also decreases capillary leakage, reduces swelling, and prevents clotting by modulating thrombin and plasmin activity. Compression is applied using elastic bandages or specially designed boots. Patients should wear the maximum level of compression they find comfortable. The type of dressing beneath the compression does not significantly affect outcomes, and simple low-adherent dressings are as effective as hydrocolloid dressings. Pentoxifylline has been shown to be an effective adjunct to compression therapy for venous ulcers. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials by the Cochrane Collaboration concluded that Pentoxifylline improves healing when used with compression bandaging and may also be effective in the absence of compression. Artificial skin, composed of collagen and cultured skin cells, is another treatment option. It provides growth factors that promote healing. A Cochrane meta-analysis found that bilayer artificial skin, when combined with compression bandaging, significantly increases the likelihood of venous ulcer healing compared to compression and simple dressings alone. Surgical correction of superficial venous reflux has also been shown to reduce ulcer recurrence. A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that surgery decreases the recurrence of ulcers at four years and increases the proportion of ulcer-free time.
